title: Romans, looking back
tomorrow: can something meant for harm end up meant for good?

lines: A MAP THAT LOOKS TOO WIDE.
cards: A hospital hallway late at night: the hum of a vending machine, a phone at four percent, someone you love behind a curtain. Or a move across the country, and a map that suddenly looks very wide.
Weeks like that raise one question under all the others: can anything come between a person and God? Paul answers in a letter to strangers, and he answers with a list.

teach.b: Romans is a letter to a church Paul hasn't visited yet. He says so plainly: “For I long to see you.” It doesn't flatter anyone: “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Everyone on the same level ground. Then the turn: “But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Not after a cleanup.
In chapter eight he faces the hard things head on: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?”

Then his answer: “For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Here's the thing to tell a friend: look at how the list is built. Death and life, the whole span. Things present and things to come, all of time.
Height and depth, all of space. And then, in case anything slipped through, any other creature. For a hard week, Romans also gives something to do.
A few chapters on: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
A huge promise, then a hospital-chair instruction. Paul seems to expect the second to grow out of the first.

how: Christians read Romans in worship and study, and some learn Romans 8:38–39 by heart; it is also read at some funerals.

games.q: your friend's parents are splitting up, and she says, "maybe God gave up on our family." which reply stays with Romans 8?
o: nothing in Paul's list, not things present or to come, can separate her from God's love.
God stays close only to families that hold together.
it's a test; if she prays harder, it will stop.
games.why: Paul crosses out death and life, present and future, height and depth, and any other creature. then: weep with them that weep.

practice: Say Paul's line out loud, slowly, one pair at a time: neither death, nor life; nor things present, nor things to come; nor height, nor depth. At each pair, let one real worry of yours stand beside it.
If you pray, end with his last words, the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord; if not, simply let the list be said.

wordCard.voice: Romans. Paul's letter to a church he longed to see: all on level ground, and nothing able to separate us from the love of God.

orig.note: the Greek for 'I am persuaded' in Romans 8:38: a settled conviction.

carryVoice: The line to keep: nothing can separate us, not height, not depth, not the miles in between. Until tomorrow.
